title: ICLR 2034 quick harvest — signal compression & KV-quant notes
content:
Topline: grabbed 4 papers from ICLR poster session + a couple workshop talks that feel directly actionable for our Optimize stack. This doc is a messy harvest — things to try, quick sketches for evals, and product implications.

1) Signal Sparsity for Long-Context LMs (poster) — main idea: compress prefix activations into a sparse basis before KV insertion.
- claim: for real conversations there is substantial redundancy in KV entries; sparse projection reduces memory by ~3–6x with <1 pt drop on next-token for short prompts.
- notes: they do an online OMP-ish projection per incoming chunk (128 tokens) into learned basis (k=64). Seems expensive but they pipeline projection with tokenization -> usable for high-throughput if done on CPU with batching.
- quick experiment idea: integrate as optional pre-KV stage in our runtime. Measure throughput for typical webchat load (p95 request size ~90 tokens). Metric: effective memory reduction vs p90 latency cost.
- open questions:
  - how does basis drift across domains? they show domain-adaptive fine-tuning but we need a default basis for multi-tenant hosted API.
  - failure modes: does compression remove rare but crucial facts? need targeted pass/fail evals (QA precision on red-team prompts).

2) Adaptive KV Quantization (oral) — main idea: mixed per-key quant bits determined by estimated information score.
- they score keys using a small predictor net and dynamically allocate bits (1–8 bits). Overall compression ~2–4x with careful retraining.
- product tie-in: could be a profile in Redwood Optimize ("kv-adaptive-quant"). For Dedicated/private, allow customers to opt in.
- implementation sketch:
  - score predictor can be a tiny MLP on key-summary (first/last token embedding + mass). Run at insertion time, threshold schedule.
  - fallback rule: when predictor uncertain, store higher-precision; that keeps graceful degradation.
- experiment: measure downstream generation quality on LM-Metrics set (perplexity + instruction-following eval). Also measure CPU/GPU decomposition cost: predictor on CPU, quant kernels on device.

3) Cascade Caching (workshop talk) — multi-tier prefix cache: L1 (hot small, GPU), L2 (compressed mid, CPU RAM), L3 (ssd-backed compressed).
- interesting: they route by a combined score of recency+utility-estimate. On read, a cheap predictor attempts to reconstruct top-K tokens from compressed tiers to avoid full GPU reads.
- Redwood implications: map to our Dedicated pools + cold storage. Could reduce cross-GPU churn for large-models with huge KV footprints.
- immediate experiment: simulate with production logs (ask infra for 72h of anonymized KV access traces). Build offline simulator that implements eviction + cascade tiers; run cost/latency tradeoffs.

4) Latency-aware batching heuristics (poster) — very practical: they show that small delays (1–3ms) to await other in-flight requests significantly increase batch formation and lower p99 in many workloads.
- they propose an adaptive deadline per connection based on historical arrival rates and backoff when hitting SLO.
- cross-check with Redwood serving: our continuous batching already does similar but this paper has a simpler light-weight estimator that could be computed in the routing layer (before hitting GPU).
- action: PR idea to router: add adaptive batching window that uses exponential smoothing on arrival rate per-client-subnet. Run A/B on Hosted API for low-traffic keys.

Notes to self / todo list:
- [ ] Request anonymized KV access logs from infra (ticket to infra-team: INF-7850). Needed fields: timestamp, model, tenant_hash, key_size, access_size.
- [ ] Spike: implement their sparse projection in PyTorch as CPU batched op; microbench on a T4/CPU host. (assign: me + Ravi)
- [ ] Prototype kv-adaptive-quant predictor as a tiny TF/ONNX model; aim: <0.5ms per insertion on CPU. (assign: Sofia)
- [ ] Offline simulator for cascade caching (assign: me); target: compare cost for 3 tier configs.
- [ ] Discuss product policy for default bases and opt-in in hosted API: schedule 1-pager for product-hosted-api.

Sketch for small eval battery (for PRs):
- Dataset: mix of 1) internal convo logs (anonymized), 2) LM-Eval subset for QA + instruction-following, 3) synthetic rare-fact probes.
- Metrics: token-level perplexity, instruction-response correctness (binary), tail latency (p95/p99), measured RU (RAM/GPU) per-request.
- Effect gating: require <2% drop in correctness on instruction-following for any config we ship by default.

Loose brainstorm (brain dump):
- Could we do a hybrid: compress prefix with learned basis + store adaptive-quantized residuals? That might give best of both.
- For Private deployments: allow customers to deploy per-tenant basis builders to avoid cross-tenant drift.
- For Optimize UI: show customers a slider (conserve-memory vs preserve-quality) that toggles basis-size / quant-profile and preview expected cost savings.

References and quick links (copied from session notes):
- Signal Sparsity for Long-Context LMs — arXiv link above, code: authors/ssparse-lm (python)
- Adaptive KV Quantization — slides + small demo (repo: aq-kv)
- Cascade Caching — workshop talk video (link in linked_artifacts)
- Latency batching heuristics — poster PDF in their folder

Random scraps: 
- small idea: use our rollout system to do constrained canary: gradually enable compression for 1% tenants by request-size bucket; if quality regresses revert. Could be a low-risk path.
- think about fallbacks: if reconstruction confidence < threshold, run full read path (slower but correct).

End notes: messy but useful. Next step: sync with Ravi and Sofia next Wed (2024-02-14) to carve up spikes. Put short agenda in calendar invite: 30m.
